task.title: Variable and color fonts
task.shortdesc: Variable fonts can change their design along axes such as weight, width or optical size. Color fonts can draw glyphs with indexed colors from a palette. The font file must provide the axis or palette that you request.

info.p: CSS Fonts 4 §8.1, Optical sizing control.
An optical-size axis lets a font adjust glyph details for different text sizes. The property accepts auto or none .

With auto, the processor may adjust glyphs for the used font size. Variable OpenType and TrueType fonts commonly do this through the opsz axis. The processor must stay within the axis range in the font and must not synthesize optical sizing when the font does not provide it. With none, it must not change glyph shapes for optical size.
CSS Fonts 4 §8.2, Low-level font variation settings control.

Use this property to set one or more variable-font axes directly. Each item is a four-character, case-sensitive <opentype-tag> followed by a number. The tag must contain printable ASCII characters, from U+0020 through U+007E. The number may be fractional or negative.

normal means this property makes no change to glyph shape, matching or positioning. An unknown axis tag or an axis not supported by the selected font has no effect. A number outside the supported range for an axis is clamped to that range. If a tag occurs more than once, its last value is used.

Use higher-level properties for common axes. font-weight controls the wght axis, font-width controls wdth, font-style controls slnt or ital, and font-optical-sizing controls opsz. These properties participate in font matching; font-variation-settings does not.
CSS Fonts 4 §9.1, Controlling color font palettes.
Use this property to choose the colors used by a color font. It accepts normal , light , dark , a named palette, or palette-mix() .

ul.li: normal uses the font’s normal palette selection. For OpenType CPAL fonts, this is usually palette index 0. When color-scheme requests a light or dark scheme, the specification says the processor should select the first matching palette.
light selects the first palette marked for light backgrounds. If the font format has no such metadata, or no palette is marked, this behaves as normal.
dark selects the first palette marked for dark backgrounds. If the font format has no such metadata, or no palette is marked, this behaves as normal.

A palette identifier names an author-defined palette from @font-palette-values. The identifier is a <dashed-ident> , so it starts with two hyphens, as in --night. If no applicable rule defines it, it behaves as normal.

palette-mix() makes a palette by interpolating corresponding colors from one or more other palettes. Its arguments are font-palette values, which may be keywords, named palettes or nested palette-mix() functions. Each may have a percentage from 0% to 100%. Omitted percentages share the remaining percentage equally. If specified percentages total more than 100%, they are normalized; if they total less, the result’s opacity is reduced by the unassigned share. The rules follow CSS Color 5 §3.2 and color-mix() .

info.p: For example, palette-mix(in oklab, dark 25%, --night) blends one quarter of the dark palette with three quarters of --night. The optional <color-interpolation-method> selects the space used to blend corresponding colors. If omitted, the default is oklab.

ul.li: Rectangular RGB spaces include srgb , srgb-linear , display-p3 , display-p3-linear , a98-rgb , prophoto-rgb and rec2020 . The -linear forms interpolate light rather than gamma-encoded channel values.
lab and oklab use lightness and two opponent-color coordinates. The xyz spaces use CIE XYZ tristimulus coordinates: xyz, xyz-d50 and xyz-d65 identify the reference white.
Polar spaces represent colors with an angle and other coordinates. hsl uses hue, saturation and lightness. hwb uses hue, whiteness and blackness. lch and oklch use lightness, chroma and hue.

A polar space may also specify a hue direction using shorter , longer , increasing or decreasing . shorter follows the shorter route around the hue circle, longer the longer route, increasing moves toward larger hue angles, and decreasing moves toward smaller hue angles. If no direction is written, shorter is used. See the color interpolation grammar for the complete syntax.

info.p: CSS Fonts 4 §9.2, User-defined font color palettes.

Use this rule to give a palette a name, choose its starting palette and replace selected colors. Its name must be a <dashed-ident>, such as --night. When rules use the same name, the last rule in document order takes effect.

The rule requires a font-family descriptor. It accepts one or more named font families, separated by commas. A family name may be a string or a sequence of identifiers, such as "Example Emoji" or Example Sans. Generic family names such as serif are not allowed. The palette applies only to font faces whose family name matches.
CSS Fonts 4 §9.2.2, Specifying the base palette.
This descriptor chooses the palette in the font on which the named palette is based.

ul.li: light selects the first palette marked for light backgrounds. If the font format has no such metadata, or no palette is marked, it means palette index 0.
dark selects the first palette marked for dark backgrounds. If the font format has no such metadata, or no palette is marked, it means palette index 0.
A non-negative integer selects a zero-based palette index. For example, 0 selects the first palette and 2 selects the third.

info.p: If this descriptor is omitted, or the font has no palette at that index, the base is palette 0. Colors not replaced by override-colors remain from the base palette.
CSS Fonts 4 §9.2.3, Overriding colors from a palette.
This descriptor takes a comma-separated list of palette entries and replacement colors. Each entry is a non-negative integer followed by an absolute CSS color. Palette indexes start at 0.

Each pair replaces the color at that index in the base palette. An index outside the palette’s range is ignored. If an index is specified more than once, the last color is used. Every color in the descriptor must be absolute, meaning its computed value has a colorimetric meaning independent of the current text color or color mode. Named colors, hexadecimal colors, and numeric rgb() colors are examples. currentColor, system colors, light-dark(), contrast-color() and device-cmyk() are not absolute. A non-absolute color makes the descriptor invalid. Wrapping a relative color in color-mix() or relative color syntax does not make it absolute. An absolute color may use any supported color space.

Math functions, var() and env() may be used in descriptor values. They are evaluated in the root element’s context. When a descriptor occurs more than once in one rule, the last valid declaration is used.
